Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 31, verses 6–7:

The Almighty's words: ﴿And among people is one who purchases idle tales﴾ (lahw al-hadith). Concerning this there are seven interpretations:

First: the purchasing of singing-girls (al-mughaniyat). This is based on the narration of al-Qasim ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "It is not lawful to sell singing-girls, nor to buy them, nor to trade in them, nor is their price (lawful)." It was concerning them that Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And among people is one who purchases idle tales﴾.

Second: singing (al-ghina'). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

Third: that it is the drum (al-tabl), said by Abd al-Karim; and the flute (al-mizmar), said by Ibn Zakhr.

Fourth: that it is falsehood (al-batil), said by Ata'.

Fifth: that it is associating partners with Allah (al-shirk billah), said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

Sixth: whatever diverts from Allah, the Glorified, said by al-Hasan.

Seventh: that it is disputation concerning the religion and immersion in falsehood, said by Sahl ibn Abd Allah.

(p-329) It is possible, if no explicit text is established concerning it, to take an eighth interpretation: that it is sorcery, gambling and soothsaying.

Regarding who was the subject of the revelation, there are two opinions:

One: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to sit in Mecca. Whenever the Quraysh said that Muhammad had said such and such, he would laugh at it, and he would relate to them the tale of Rustam and Isfandiyar, saying to them: "My tale is better than the Qur'an of Muhammad." This is related by al-Farra' and al-Kalbi.

Two: it was revealed concerning a man from the Quraysh who bought a singing slave-girl, and people became occupied with her instead of following the Prophet (ﷺ). This is related by Ibn Isa.

﴿to lead astray from the way of Allah without knowledge﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: to turn away from the religion of Allah, said by al-Tabari.

Two: to prevent recitation of the Qur'an, said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿without knowledge﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: without proof.

Two: without transmission (riwayah).

﴿and takes it in mockery﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: he takes the way of Allah as a mockery, denying it, said by Qatadah. "The way of Allah" is His religion.

Two: he mocks at it, said by al-Kalbi.

﴿For such there is a humiliating punishment﴾, i.e., one that degrades.(p-330)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 31, verse 8–11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾, concerning this there are two opinions:

One: there are pillars that you cannot see. This was said by ʿIkrimah and Mujahid.

The second: they were created without any pillars. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, meaning mountains.

﴿Lest it shake with you﴾, meaning lest it shake with you. Concerning this there are two views:

One: its meaning is that it should not move away with you. This was said by al-Naqqash.

The second: that it should not move with you. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

It is also said that the earth used to sway like a ship, so Allah anchored it with the mountains, and that they are nineteen mountains which spread out within the earth until they became stakes for it, and so it became stable. Abu al-Ashhab related from al-Hasan who said: When Allah created the earth, it began to sway. When the angels saw what the earth was doing, they said: "Our Lord, no creation can remain upon its back." So in the morning He had tied it down with the mountains. When the angels saw what the earth had been anchored with, they marvelled and said: "O our Lord, have You created a creation that is stronger than the mountains?" He said: "Yes, the wind." They said: "Have You created a creation that is stronger than the wind?" He said: "Yes, the son of Adam."

﴿And He spread throughout it every kind of moving creature﴾. Concerning this there are three views:

One of them: and He created in it, said by al-Suddi.

The second: and He spread out, said by al-Kalbi.

The third: He scattered in it every kind of moving creature, and the moving creature is the animal, so called because of its crawling (dabib), and dabib is movement.

﴿And We send down from the sky water, and We cause to grow in it every noble pair﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: they are the people; the people are the growth of the earth. Whoever enters Paradise is noble, and whoever enters the Fire is base. This was said by al-Shaʿbi.

The second: the growth of the earth is its trees and its crops, and the pair (zawj) is the type (nawʿ).

Concerning "noble" (karim) there are three views:

(p-331) One of them: that it is the good (al-hasan). This was said by Qatadah.

The second: that it is the one with good fruit. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

The third: that it is the ripe (al-yaniʿ). This was said by Ibn Kamil.

And it may admit a fourth: that "noble" is that whose price is high due to the preciousness of its worth.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 31, verse 12:

One: that he was a prophet. This was said by ʿIkrimah and al-Shaʿbi.

The second: that he was a sage (ḥakīm) and not a prophet. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said, and Isma'il said: Luqman was one of the black people of Egypt, thick-lipped. Allah gave him wisdom (al-ḥikmah) and withheld prophethood from him.

Qatadah said: Allah gave Luqman the choice between prophethood and wisdom, and he chose wisdom over prophethood. Then Jibril came to him while he was asleep and sprinkled wisdom upon him, and he woke up speaking it. It was said to him: "How did you choose wisdom over prophethood when your Lord had given you the choice?" He said: "If He had sent prophethood to me as a firm command, I would have hoped for help from Him in it, and I would have hoped to be able to carry it out. But He gave me a choice, so I feared that I would be too weak for prophethood, and wisdom was dearer to me."

There is a difference of opinion regarding his lineage, on two views:

One: that he was from the Nubians, short and flat-nosed. This was said by Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah.

The second: he was an Abyssinian slave. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

There is a difference of opinion regarding his occupation, on three views:

The first: that he was a tailor in Egypt. This was said by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib.

The second: that he was a shepherd. A man who knew him before that saw him and said: "Are you not the slave of the Banu so-and-so who used to herd sheep yesterday?" He said: "Yes." The man said: "What brought you to what I see?" He said: "The decree of Allah, my fulfilment of trust, truthfulness in speech, and my leaving what does not concern me." This was said by ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Jabir.

The third: that he was a carpenter. His master said to him: "Slaughter a sheep for me and bring me its two best morsels." He brought him the tongue and the heart. He said to him: "There was nothing in it better than these two." He fell silent. Then he ordered him, and he slaughtered another sheep for him. Then he said: "Throw away its two worst morsels." He threw away the tongue and the heart. He said to him: "I ordered you to bring me the two best morsels, and you brought me the tongue and the heart; and I ordered you to throw away its two worst morsels, and you threw away the tongue and the heart." He said: "There is nothing better than these two when they are good, and nothing worse than them when they are bad." This was said by Khalid al-Rabaʿi.

There is a difference of opinion regarding his time, on two views:

One: that he lived between ʿIsa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both.

The second: that he was a son of Kush ibn Sam ibn Nuh. He was born in the tenth year of the reign of Dawud, peace be upon him, and he lived until the time of Yunus, peace be upon him.

Regarding the ﴿wisdom﴾ which he was given, there are three sayings:

The first: that it is understanding and intellect. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: jurisprudence, intellect, and correctness in speech. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: trustworthiness.

﴿That give thanks to Allah﴾, meaning the favours of Allah. Regarding this there are two aspects:

The first: the meaning of the statement is: "We certainly gave him wisdom, and We gave him thankfulness to Allah." This was said by al-Mufaddal.

The second: "We gave him wisdom so that he would give thanks to Allah." This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding his thankfulness there are four aspects:

The first: it is praising Him for His favours.

The second: it is not disobeying Him with His favours.

The third: it is not seeing a partner with Him in His favours upon him.

The fourth: it is obeying Him in what He commanded.

﴿And whoever gives thanks, he gives thanks only for his own self﴾, i.e., his thanks returns to his own self, because when he increases in thankfulness for the favour, it benefits him.

﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾: regarding this there are two aspects:

The first: meaning he disbelieves in Allah and the Last Day. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the disbelief of favour (kufr al-niʿmah), said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

﴿Then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾: regarding this there are two aspects:

The first: Free of need from His creation, Praiseworthy in His action. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The second: Free of need from their thanks, and praised by His creation. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 31, verses 13–15:

﴿And when Luqman said to his son﴾, meaning: O Muhammad, recall the statement of Luqman to his son. Regarding the name of his son there are three opinions:

First: Mushkim, related by al-Kalbi.

Second: An'um, related by al-Naqqash.

Third: Babaan.

﴿while he was admonishing him﴾, meaning: reminding him and disciplining him.

﴿"O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great injustice."﴾ Meaning: in the sight of Allah. It is called injustice because the one who associates has wronged himself by it. It is said that he said this to his son while the son was a polytheist. His words "O my son" are not literally a diminutive, though they are in its form; rather, they are said out of tenderness, as one says to a man "O my brother."

For a small boy, it is *kuwayyis* (a diminutive of endearment).

The Exalted said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man [regarding] his parents﴾, meaning: goodness and tenderness toward them both.

Regarding this verse there are two opinions:

First: It is general, even though it came in a specific wording, and what is intended is all people. This is related by Ibn Kamil.

Second: It is specific to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who was enjoined regarding his parents. His father's name was Malik, and his mother's name was Hamna bint Abi Sufyan ibn Umayya. This is related by al-Naqqash.

﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

First: its meaning is hardship upon hardship, related by Ibn Abbas.

Second: exertion upon exertion, related by Qatada.

Third: weakness upon weakness, related by al-Hasan and Ata'.

From the verse of Qa'nab ibn Umm Sahib:

*Is there for the blamers one who forbids them, so that he restrains them?*
*Indeed, the blamers in it are weariness and exhaustion.*

Here "weakness" means frailty.

Then, according to this interpretation, there are three possibilities:

First: the weakness of the child upon the weakness of the mother, related by Mujahid.

Second: the weakness of the father's seed upon the weakness of the mother's seed, related by Ibn Bahr.

Third: the weakness of the child, stage after stage. Its weakness as a drop (*nutfah*), then a clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then a complete bone, then a newborn, then an infant, then one weaned. This is related by Abu Kamil.

A fourth possibility is also conceivable: the weakness of the body upon the weakness of resolve.

﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾. By weaning (*fisal*) is meant ceasing to be nursed with milk.

There is disagreement about whether the ruling of suckling (*al-rida'*, nursing that establishes prohibited relations of marriage) after the two years is the same as its ruling within the two years, with four opinions:

[p. 335] First: It does not establish prohibition after the two years, even by the blink of an eye, because Allah set the term at two years, and because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no suckling after the two years." This is the opinion of al-Shafi'i.

Second: It establishes prohibition for some days after the two years. This is the opinion of Malik.

Third: It establishes prohibition for six months after the two years, completing thirty months, based on His saying: ﴿And his carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. This is the opinion of Abu Hanifa.

Fourth: Its prohibition is not limited by a fixed period, and it establishes prohibition for an adult just as it does for a child. This is the opinion of some of the people of Madina.

﴿"Give thanks to Me and to your parents."﴾ Meaning: give thanks to Me for the blessing, and to your parents for their upbringing.

Thanks to Allah is through praise and obedience, and thanks to the parents is through goodness and maintaining ties. Qatada said: Allah distinguished between His right and the right of the parents, saying: "Give thanks to Me and to your parents."

﴿To Me is the final return﴾, meaning: the return is to Allah, who will reward the doer of good with Paradise and the doer of evil with the Fire.

[p. 336] Ata' related from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The pleasure of the Lord is from the pleasure of the parent, and the anger of the Lord is from the anger of the parent."

[p. 337] The Exalted said: ﴿And if they strive with you﴾, meaning: they urge you.

﴿to associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾. Its meaning: you do not know that I have a partner.

﴿then do not obey them﴾, meaning: in polytheism.

﴿but accompany them in this world with kindness﴾, meaning: seeking reward (*ihtisaban*).

Qatada said: Visit them when they are ill, follow their funerals when they die, and provide for them from what Allah the Exalted has given you.

﴿And follow the way of those who turn back to Me﴾. Yahya ibn Salam said: those who turn to Him with sincere hearts, namely the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers.

Mus'ab ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas related: Sa'd's mother swore that she would not eat or drink until Sa'd turned away from his religion. He refused her, and she remained in that state until she fainted. Then she invoked Allah against him, and Allah revealed this verse concerning him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"O my son, indeed it, if it should be the weight of a mustard seed"﴾. This is a parable struck for the weight of a mustard seed.

Qatadah said: "of good or evil."

﴿"and be within a rock"﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: it is the rock beneath the seventh earth. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Suddi.

Abdullah ibn al-Harith said: "It is a rock on the back of the fish." al-Thawri said: "It has reached us that the greenness of the sky comes from that rock." Ibn Abbas said: "This rock is neither in the heavens nor in the earth."

[p-338 continues] It has also been said that this rock is Sijjin (the register) in which the deeds of the disbelievers are written, and it is not raised to the heavens.

The second: the meaning of his saying "within a rock" is "within a mountain." This was said by Qatadah.

﴿"or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth"﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: by requiting whatever good or evil matched it in weight.

The second: Allah knows it, and He brings it forth when He wills. Likewise, a small deed of good or evil, Allah knows it and recompenses for it.

﴿"Indeed Allah is Subtle"﴾ in extracting it.

﴿"Aware"﴾ of its place. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Ali ibn Rabah al-Lakhmi narrated, saying: When Luqman admonished his son with this, he took a mustard seed and brought it to the sea and cast it into its depths. Then he remained as long as he willed, then he remembered it and extended his hand, and Allah sent a fly which snatched it and carried it until it placed it in his hand.

The first: over the harm that befalls you in commanding good and forbidding evil.

The second: over the trial that befalls you in yourself or your property.

The first: what Allah has commanded among affairs.

The second: of the controlling of affairs. This was said by al-Mufaddal.

Concerning ʿazm (resolve) and ḥazm (firm judgment) there are two opinions:

The first: their meaning is one, even though their wording differs.

The second: their meanings differ, and concerning their difference there are two views:

The second: because the cry of every creature is glorification of Allah, except the donkey, which cries out when it sees Satan. This was said by Sufyan al-Thawri. It is related from Bishr ibn al-Harith that he said: "The braying of the donkey is a supplication against the oppressors."

The reason Allah struck the voice of the donkey as a parable is what Sulayman ibn Arqam narrated from al-Hasan: that the polytheists in the Jahiliyyah used to boast and show off by raising their voices. Whoever among them had the louder voice was the more honoured, and whoever had the lower voice was the more humiliated. So Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿"Indeed the most hateful of voices is the braying of donkeys"﴾, meaning: if there were a thing feared for its voice, it would be the donkey; so He placed them in the parable in its rank.[p-342]

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 31, verse 20–21:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. Regarding His subjecting them, there are two aspects:

One: facilitating them (tashhil).

The second: benefiting from them (al-intifa').

﴿And He has completed upon you His favours﴾. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs read it without tanwin (nin), in the plural form (niʿam), while the rest read it with tanwin, meaning one favour (niʿmah wahidah). In this reading there are two aspects:

One: that it refers to Islam, and so made it singular; this was said by Ibrahim.

The second: that it intends abundance by means of the singular form, like the saying of the Arabs: "The dinar and the dirham have multiplied," and "The land is a sword and a horse." This is more emphatic in expressing abundance than the plural form; this was said by Ibn Shajara.

And regarding His saying: ﴿apparent and hidden﴾, there are five opinions:

One of them: that the apparent is Islam, and the hidden is what Allah has concealed of sins; this was said by Muqatil.

The second: that the apparent is on the tongue, and the hidden is in the heart; this was said by Mujahid and Waki'.

The third: that the apparent is the adornment and clothing He gave them, and the hidden is the household goods; this was related by al-Naqqash.

The fifth: the apparent is offspring, and the hidden is intercourse.

And it is possible (yahtamilu) as a sixth: that the apparent is in one's own self, and the hidden is in his descendants after him.

And it is possible as a seventh: that the apparent is what has passed, and the hidden is what is yet to come.

And it is possible as a ninth: that the apparent is in the bodies, and the hidden is in the religions.

﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

One of them: "It was revealed concerning a Jew who came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about your Lord, of what is He made?' Then a thunderbolt came and seized him."

The second: that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to say that the angels are the daughters of Allah; this was said by Abu Malik.

The words of God: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾, and the verse continues.

There are two reports concerning the occasion of its revelation:

The first: what Sa'id narrated from Qatadah, that the polytheists said, "It is only speech," meaning the Qur'an, "that is about to run out." So God revealed this verse, meaning: even if the trees of the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven seas added to it, were ink, the pens would break and the waters of the seas would run dry before the wonders of my Lord, His wisdom, and His knowledge run out.

The second: what Ibn 'Abbas narrated, that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Medina, the rabbis of the Jews said to him: "O Muhammad, what do you mean by your saying: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra' 85]? Do you mean us, or your people?" He said: "Each of you has not been given of knowledge except a little, you and they." They said: "But you recite in what has come to you from God that we have been given the Torah, and in it is an explanation of everything." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is, in the knowledge of God, a little." Then this verse was revealed.

The meaning of ﴿yamuddu﴾ is: He adds to it one thing after another. It is said of an increase, "madadtuhu," and of help, "amdadtuhu."

﴿The words of God would not run out﴾. Nafad (running out) of a thing is the perishing of its last part after the perishing of its first part, so it is not said of what has perished entirely that it "nafida."

First: they are the blessings of God upon the people of His obedience in Paradise.

Second: they are the kinds of His creatures.

Third: all that He has decreed in the Preserved Tablet concerning the affairs of His creation.

Fourth: they are the knowledge of God.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 31, verses 29–30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night?﴾ On this there are three views:

First: He takes from the summer to the winter and takes from the winter to the summer. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid.

Second: He reduces from the day to place it in the night, and reduces from the night to place it in the day. This was said by al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

Third: He makes the darkness travel the paths of the light and makes the light travel the paths of the darkness, so that each of them becomes in the place of the other. This was said by Ibn Shajarah.

It may also admit a fourth view: that He causes the darkness of the night to enter into the light of the day when it approaches, and causes the light of the day to enter into the darkness of the night when it approaches, so that each of them becomes entering into the other.

(p-346) ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning He made them subservient through their rising and setting, as a determination of the terms and a completion of the benefits.

﴿Each runs to a term appointed﴾. On this there are two views:

One: meaning, to its time in its rising and setting, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. This is the meaning of Qatadah's saying.

Second: until the Day of Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, meaning, with what you do by night and by day.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾. On this there are three views:

First: He is Allah, there is no god other than Him. This was said by Ibn Kamil.

Second: that "the Truth" is one of the names of Allah. This was said by Abu Salih.

Third: that Allah is the one who judges by the truth.

It may also admit a fourth view: that obedience to Allah is the truth.

﴿And that what they call upon besides Him is falsehood﴾. On this there are two views:

One: Satan is the falsehood. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: what they associated with Allah, exalted is He, of idols and images. This was said by Ibn Kamil.

﴿And that Allah is the Most High, the Most Great﴾, meaning, the Most High in His station, the Most Great in His authority. (p-347)

Al-Mawardi's commentary on Surah 31, verses 31–32:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you not see that the ships sail upon the sea by the favour of God﴾ admits of two meanings:

One: by God's mercy toward you in your deliverance from it.

The second: by God's favour upon you in your benefit from it.

﴿That He may show you of His signs﴾ has three interpretations:

One: it means the sailing of the ships upon it. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam. Al-Hasan said: "The key to the seas is the ships, the key to the earth is the roads, and the key to the sky is supplication."

The second: what you witness of God's power in it. This was said by Ibn Shajara.

The third: what God provides you from it. This was said by al-Naqqash.

﴿For every steadfast, grateful one﴾ has two meanings:

One: steadfast in trial, grateful in blessings.

The second: steadfast in obedience, grateful for the reward.

Al-Sha'bi said: "Patience is half of faith, gratitude is half of faith, and certainty is the whole of faith. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾ and His saying: ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who are certain﴾?"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when a wave covers them like shade-canopies﴾ has two meanings:

One: like clouds. This was said by Qatada.

The second: like mountains. This was said by al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Salam.

As for its likening to shade (ẓulal), there are two meanings:

One: for its blackness. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

The second: for its immensity.

(p-348) ﴿Calling upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ means: affirming His oneness, not calling upon anyone other than Him for their deliverance.

﴿But when He delivers them to the land﴾ means: from the sea.

﴿Among them is a moderate one﴾ has three interpretations:

One: its meaning is one who is just in his covenant, who fulfils on land what he pledged to God at sea. This was said by al-Naqqash.

The second: that he is the believer who holds firmly to monotheism and obedience. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: that he is moderate in his speech while being a disbeliever. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿None denies Our signs except every treacherous ingrate﴾ has two meanings:

One: that he is the one who denies. This was said by 'Atiyya.

The second, which is the view of the majority: that he is the treacherous betrayer. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

"Indeed, if you saw Abu 'Umayr,
you would fill your hands with treachery and perfidy."

Denial of the signs (juḥd al-āyāt) is rejecting their very substance, and jaḥd with the signs is denying their indications and proofs.

The second: for its immensity.

(p-348) ﴿Calling upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ means: affirming His oneness, not calling upon anyone other than Him for their deliverance.

﴿But when He delivers them to the land﴾ means: from the sea.

﴿Among them is a moderate one﴾ has three interpretations:

One: its meaning is one who is just in his covenant, who fulfils on land what he pledged to God at sea. This was said by al-Naqqash.

The second: that he is the believer who holds firmly to monotheism and obedience. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: that he is moderate in his speech while being a disbeliever. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿None denies Our signs except every treacherous ingrate﴾ has two meanings:

One: that he is the one who denies. This was said by 'Atiyya.

The second, which is the view of the majority: that he is the treacherous betrayer. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

"Indeed, if you saw Abu 'Umayr,
you would fill your hands with treachery and perfidy."

Denial of the signs (juḥd al-āyāt) is rejecting their very substance, and jaḥd with the signs is denying their indications and proofs.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 31, verse 33:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no father will avail anything for his child﴾ has three interpretations:

(p-349) The first: its meaning is "no father will suffice for his child" (la yughni). It is said: "jazaytu 'anka" with the meaning of "ughnaytu 'anka" (I sufficed for you / I was adequate on your behalf). This is what Ibn 'Isa said.

The second: "no father will settle on behalf of his child" (la yaqdi), that is, will pay his debt. This is what al-Mufaddal and Ibn Kamil said.

The third: "no father will bear on behalf of his child" (la yahmil). al-Ra'i said:

"And I bore the affair of all the worlds, and none could bear it except the perfect and the son of the perfect."

That is, "I bore (it)."

﴿Nor will a child avail anything for his father at all. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ meaning the resurrection and the recompense.

﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾ may carry two meanings:

The first: let not the delay of retribution deceive you.

The second: let not wealth deceive you away from Islam.

﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾. It is recited in two ways:

The first: with a ḍamma (al-ghurūru).

The second: with a fatḥa (al-gharūru), which is the reading of the majority.

As for its interpretation with a ḍamma, there are two views:

The first: that the Deceiver (al-ghurūr) is Satan. This is said by Mujahid.

The second: false hope, which is wishing for forgiveness while engaged in disobedience. This is said by Ibn Jubayr.

It may also bear a third meaning: that you hide from Allah what you conceal of acts of disobedience.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 31, verse 34:

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ admits of two meanings:

One of them: that its establishment is specific to His knowledge.

The second: that its establishment is contingent upon His will.

﴿And He sends down the rain﴾ at whatever time and place He wills.

﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾. In this there are two meanings:

One of them: whether male or female, healthy or sick.

The second: whether believer or disbeliever, wretched or blessed.

﴿And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾. In this there are two meanings:

One of them: whether good or evil.

The second: whether faith or disbelief.

﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾. In this there are two meanings:

One of them: under what ruling it will die, whether happiness or wretchedness; this is related from al-Naqqash.

The second: in what land its death and burial will occur, and this is the more apparent.

Abu Malih related from Abu 'Izzah al-Hudhali, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah, exalted is He, wishes to take the soul of a servant in a land, He makes for him a need in it, and he does not stop until he arrives there." Then he (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ up to His saying: ﴿in what land it will die﴾.

Hilal ibn Isaf said: No child is born except that in his navel is some of the soil of the land in which he will be buried.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing, Acquainted﴾. This admits of two meanings:

One of them: Knowing of the unseen, Acquainted with the intention.

The second: Knowing of the deeds, Acquainted with the recompense.

It is said that this verse was revealed concerning a man from the desert dwellers called al-Warith ibn 'Amr ibn Harithah, who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My wife is pregnant, so inform me what she will bear. Our land is barren, so inform me when the rain will come down. I know when I was born, so inform me when the Hour will be established." So this verse was revealed.

And Allah knows best.
